newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iomega demos data disk for future camera, phone.
newsitem.headline: Iomega demos data disk for future camera, phone.

text.p: With tens of thousands of consumers due at the CeBIT trade fair this weekend, data storage group Iomega Corp prepared to give them a glimpse of technolgy that could revolutionise some of the top selling electronics gear.

The company was demonstrating its n*hand miniature computer disk that could store 200 pictures in future digital cameras, voice mail and phone numbers in mobile phones and data and software in palmtop PCs, the company said.
N*hand, while only slightly larger than a match book, can hold 20 megabytes of data -- the same as 14 of today's standard floppy disks.

"We think you will most likely see products using n*hand in the first quarter of 1998," Iomega marketing chief Tim Hill told Reuters. "The next turn of digital cameras, mobile phones and palmtops should have some."

Hill said the drives that read n*hand disks could add $100 or so to cameras, phones or palmtops. The n*hand disks would cost consumers about $15 each, giving them a way to store hundreds of pictures or several weeks of messages, he said.

The company also said it recently sold its five millionth ZIP drive, a device for personal computers that stores 100 megabytes of information on removable disks that are only a bit thicker than the 1.44 megabyte floppies computer users have now.
Iomega, whose sales have soared tenfold to $1.2 billion in 1996 since the ZIP drive came out in 1993, saw great potential for n*hand, but said it might not duplicate ZIP growth.
"With ZIP, there was an installed base of people who could use the product," Hill said in an interview. "N*hand is breaking into new areas where this kind of device hasnt been used yet."

The company, which at CeBIT said Computer 2000 AG and Ingram Micro had signed on as European distributors, also had a 200 megbyte ZIP drive working in its lab, but did not plan to release it any time soon.

"We are going to focus on driving down the price of our current product," said CEO Kim Edwards. "We don't intend to offer the next version of it until we see a change in the market or encroachment from competition."
Iomega aimed to reduce the price of a ZIP drive over the next year or so to $99, from the current $299 level, he said.
ZIP sales have soared as Dell Computer Corp, Gateway 2000 Inc, Apple Computer Inc and others have offered them as options on their business PCs.
Their only competition comes from another standard called LS-120 that has fewer backers. One is Compaq Computer Corp., the world's largest PC maker, although Compaq also offers ZIP drives as options.
"Compaq is splitting the difference to see which technology does best in the marketplace, and so far we are well ahead," Hill said.
